content.study_question: Can a CT-based radiomic risk score identify which reverse shoulder patients are most at risk for instability?
story: Instability is the most common complication and reason for revision after reverse total shoulder arthroplasty (rTSA). Many risk factors are known, but most patients carry several of them at once, so it is hard to tell who is truly at risk.

Elwell, Roche and colleagues analyzed {n_clinical} primary rTSA patients from {n_sites} sites in the Equinoxe multicenter database, including pre-operative CT scans from {n_ct} patients. An automated machine-learning segmentation measured the shape of each rotator cuff muscle and a bone-based instability risk score. The team then measured how risk builds as factors accumulate, and set score thresholds that sort patients into low, moderate and high risk before surgery.

key_findings.label: Instability is rare overall
key_findings.text: Instability occurred in {rate_overall} of {n_clinical} patients, and was more common in men ({rate_male}) than in women ({rate_female}).

key_findings.label: Almost everyone carries risk
key_findings.text: Only {share_zero_rf} of patients had no risk factors and {share_ge5_rf} had five or more. The instability rate climbed from {rate_1rf} with one risk factor to {rate_13rf} with 13 or more.

key_findings.label: Seventeen risk factors, seven of them new
key_findings.text: Of the {count_rf} risk factors, {count_radiomic} come from the pre-operative CT: the shape of the supraspinatus, subscapularis and teres minor, plus the instability risk score. These are the first radiomic risk factors reported for instability after rTSA.

key_findings.label: Three clear thresholds
key_findings.text: A score below 0.3 marked low risk ({low_rate} rate, odds ratio {low_or}). A score of 0.3 to 0.6 marked moderate risk ({mod_rate}, odds ratio {mod_or}). A score above 0.6 marked high risk ({high_rate}, odds ratio {high_or}).

key_findings.label: What surgeons can change
key_findings.text: In high-risk patients, subscapularis repair, GPS navigation and a BMI of 30 or less were associated with {mod_range_low} to {mod_range_high} lower odds of instability.

content.clinical_context: The risk score turns a routine pre-operative CT into a low, moderate or high instability rating. For high-risk patients, surgeons can focus on the factors they control: repair the subscapularis whenever possible, use navigation, and address BMI. A low score can reassure surgeon and patient, even when other risk factors are present.
content.limitations: These findings are limited by short average follow-up ({fu_clinical} months clinical, {fu_ct} months CT), possible confounding of implant choices, and internal validation only. The thresholds still need external validation.

icon_list.title: The seven radiomic risk factors
icon_list.quote: supraspinatus elongation >0.317, supraspinatus flatness >0.191, supraspinatus volume >53cm3, subscapularis major axis length >132mm, subscapularis surface-to-volume ratio <0.182, teres minor flatness <0.153, and the instability risk score >0.6
